sourcedFrom: MARLIN® MODEL 1895™ AND MODEL 336™ LEVER-ACTION RIFLES INSTRUCTION MANUAL — MCLA 1/2026 R8 (document PM733) (2026)
cleanIntro: Marlin's routine strip of the Model 336 is deliberately three parts — the lever, the bolt assembly and the ejector — and the book says so in as many words. Everything that matters for reliability on this action is reachable from there: the chamber and extractor, the bolt face, the two-piece firing pin and the inside of the receiver. Two things about this rifle drive the procedure and are worth knowing before you start. First, the ejector is a loose part held in place by nothing but gravity once the bolt is out, so the receiver stays ejection-port-UP from the moment the bolt comes back. Second, the rear firing pin doubles as a safety and has to move freely and return on its own — that check is a pass/fail on whether the rifle is safe to shoot, not a nicety. The 336 is the .30-30 gun in this book and the .30-30 is a rimmed cartridge fed from a tube, which is why the unloading sequence is a full cycle-and-check rather than dropping a magazine. The Deep Clean branch takes the butt stock off and cleans the trigger and hammer IN PLACE, which is as far as this book goes.

steps.title: Lever down and forward until the bolt is fully back
steps.action: Point the Model 336 in a safe direction and rotate the lever fully downward and forward until the bolt has travelled all the way rearward. You will feel the lever stop hard at the end of its arc — that hard stop is what proves the bolt is fully back and the extractor has had its full stroke. A lazy, half-hearted throw is the classic mistake here: it can pull a live round out of the chamber and drop it straight back onto the carrier instead of throwing it clear of the rifle.
steps.quote:
1. Open the action by rotating the lever downward/forward until the bolt is
fully rearward. This will extract and eject a live cartridge or spent cartridge case in the chamber.
steps.cite: MARLIN® MODEL 1895™ AND MODEL 336™ LEVER-ACTION RIFLES INSTRUCTION MANUAL — MCLA 1/2026 R8 (document PM733) — To Unload Rifle — p.25

steps.title: Safety button fully right — the red band disappears
steps.action: Push the crossbolt safety button fully to the shooter's right and then look at it. Marlin defines the safe state by what you can no longer see rather than by which side the button sits on, and the red band is the only reliable tell — a button that is only part-way across still shows red. Check it visually every time; on a lever gun your hand is about to be inside the action.
steps.quote: 2. Engage the safety mechanism by moving the safety button fully to the shooter's right. The red band will not be visible.
steps.cite: MARLIN® MODEL 1895™ AND MODEL 336™ LEVER-ACTION RIFLES INSTRUCTION MANUAL — MCLA 1/2026 R8 (document PM733) — To Unload Rifle — p.25

steps.title: Cycle the lever until nothing more comes out
steps.action: Close the lever, open it again, and keep repeating the cycle until no further cartridge is ejected. A tube magazine feeds one round onto the carrier per stroke, so there is no single motion that empties it — the only way to empty the tube is to run every round through the action. Count them out if you loaded a known number, and keep the muzzle in a safe direction throughout.
steps.caution: 3. If the magazine is empty when the bolt is being retracted (via the lever) to extract a cartridge, the cartridge may drop on top of the carrier. Then, when the bolt moves forward, the cartridge will be chambered again! Always make sure the magazine is empty before clearing the chamber, and visually ensure that no cartridges remain in the firearm.
steps.quote: 4. Repeat steps 1 through 3 until all cartridges are ejected from the firearm (both the magazine and the chamber.) See “Correct Unloading Sequence” below.
steps.cite: MARLIN® MODEL 1895™ AND MODEL 336™ LEVER-ACTION RIFLES INSTRUCTION MANUAL — MCLA 1/2026 R8 (document PM733) — To Unload Rifle — p.25

steps.title: Eyes into the ejection port — chamber, loading port, magazine
steps.action: With the bolt held open, look into the ejection port and check three separate places: the chamber, the loading port and the magazine. This is a lever gun with a tube under the barrel, so a round can be hiding in the tube with a perfectly empty chamber. Do not accept the feel of the action as evidence — look, and keep looking until all three read empty.
steps.quote: 5. With the bolt open, look into the ejection port and visually check the chamber, loading port and magazine for cartridges, ensuring the firearm is completely unloaded.
steps.cite: MARLIN® MODEL 1895™ AND MODEL 336™ LEVER-ACTION RIFLES INSTRUCTION MANUAL — MCLA 1/2026 R8 (document PM733) — To Unload Rifle — p.25
steps.warn: NEVER assume your firearm is unloaded to justify careless handling.

steps.title: Eye protection on, covered bench, tray for small parts
steps.action: Before anything comes apart, put eye protection on and work on a covered bench. Marlin asks for a shallow-nap rug or a coarse blanket under the rifle, which is not fussiness — it stops the receiver sliding and it traps the ejector if you drop it. Have a tray or a shoebox to hand and put each part into it as it comes off.
steps.prose: The ejector on this action is a small flat part that lives loose in the receiver. On a bare bench it bounces; on a blanket it stays where it lands.
steps.quote: Unload the firearm before cleaning. Look into the ejection port and visually check the chamber and magazine to make sure there are no cartridges in the firearm. Always wear eye protection when handling, disassembling and assembling the firearm.
steps.cite: MARLIN® MODEL 1895™ AND MODEL 336™ LEVER-ACTION RIFLES INSTRUCTION MANUAL — MCLA 1/2026 R8 (document PM733) — Disassembly — p.30

steps.title: Lever half-way through its stroke, then out with the mounting screw
steps.action: Rotate the lever to about the half-way point of its stroke and stop there. That position lines the lever's pivot up with the clearance cut it needs to come out, and it is why the screw comes out second and not first. Now back the lever mounting screw out counterclockwise and set it aside where it cannot roll.
steps.prose: Try this with the lever fully closed or fully open and the lever will not clear the bolt — people then assume the screw is not all the way out and start levering, which is how the receiver gets marked.
steps.quote: 5. To remove the lever from the receiver, begin by rotating the lever half way through its stroke. 6. Remove the lever mounting screw by turning the screw counterclockwise. See Figure 14.
steps.cite: MARLIN® MODEL 1895™ AND MODEL 336™ LEVER-ACTION RIFLES INSTRUCTION MANUAL — MCLA 1/2026 R8 (document PM733) — Disassembly — p.31

steps.title: Pull the lever down and out of the bolt
steps.action: With the screw out, pull the lever downward and draw it clear of the bolt assembly and the receiver. It should come away with no force at all. If it binds, the lever is not at its half-stroke position — put it back and re-find the spot rather than pulling harder.
steps.quote: 7. Pull the lever down and remove it from the bolt assembly and receiver. See Figure 15.
steps.cite: MARLIN® MODEL 1895™ AND MODEL 336™ LEVER-ACTION RIFLES INSTRUCTION MANUAL — MCLA 1/2026 R8 (document PM733) — Disassembly — p.31

steps.title: Receiver flat, ejection port UP, bolt straight out the back
steps.action: Lay the receiver flat on the bench with the ejection port facing UP, then draw the bolt assembly rearward out of the receiver. Port-up is the whole point of the instruction: gravity is the only thing holding the ejector in its seat once the bolt is gone. Turn the rifle over at this moment and the ejector drops out somewhere you are not looking.
steps.prose: The bolt slides straight back on its rails and needs no twisting; if it snags, the lever is still partly engaged.
steps.quote:
8. With the lever removed, lay the receiver flat with the ejection port up to
maintain the position of the ejector and pull the bolt assembly rearward from the receiver. See Figure 16.
steps.cite: MARLIN® MODEL 1895™ AND MODEL 336™ LEVER-ACTION RIFLES INSTRUCTION MANUAL — MCLA 1/2026 R8 (document PM733) — To Remove the Bolt Assembly — p.32

steps.title: Lift the ejector out through the ejection port
steps.action: Take a pair of pliers and lift the ejector up and out through the ejection port. Use them to grip, not to pry — the ejector is a thin part and a bent one will not throw cases clear. Put it in the tray with the lever and its screw.
steps.quote: 9. With a pair of pliers, remove the ejector from the receiver by lifting it out through the ejection port. See Figure 17. Be careful not to damage the ejector.
steps.cite: MARLIN® MODEL 1895™ AND MODEL 336™ LEVER-ACTION RIFLES INSTRUCTION MANUAL — MCLA 1/2026 R8 (document PM733) — To Remove the Bolt Assembly — p.32

steps.title: Field strip complete — lever, bolt, ejector, and no further
steps.action: You now have four pieces on the bench: the Model 336 itself, the lever with its mounting screw, the bolt assembly and the ejector. That is the whole routine strip Marlin publishes, and it is deliberately short — for routine cleaning of this rifle only the lever, bolt and ejector come off. Marlin's ceiling on the Model 336 is explicit: a lever-action centerfire rifle is not to be taken further apart than this book describes, except by the factory. Do not chase the trigger group, the hammer or the magazine tube components.
steps.quote: 1. For routine cleaning, it is necessary only to remove the lever, bolt, and ejector.
steps.cite: MARLIN® MODEL 1895™ AND MODEL 336™ LEVER-ACTION RIFLES INSTRUCTION MANUAL — MCLA 1/2026 R8 (document PM733) — Care and Cleaning — p.33
steps.warn: CAUTION: Lever-action centerfire firearms should NOT be disassembled beyond what is described in this manual, except by the factory.

steps.title: Bore from the chamber end, brush then dry patches
steps.action: Insert the rod from the CHAMBER end and push a solvent-wet patch through until it exits the muzzle, several times. Follow with a solvent-wet brush run the full length of the bore, then dry patches until they come out clean. Never reverse the rod while a brush or patch is still inside the bore — it will turn over and bind, and getting a stuck brush out of a rifle bore is a bad afternoon.
steps.caution: THE USE OF CAUSTIC OR ACETONE-BASED CLEANERS ARE NOT RECOMMENDED AS THE SOLVENT MAY HARM THE FINISHED SURFACES, PLASTICS, LAMINATES, COMPOSITES, RUBBER GRIPS, OR OTHER MATERIALS USED IN THE CONSTRUCTION OF YOUR FIREARM.
steps.quote: 2. Push-pull a properly sized, solvent-wetted patch through the bore several times. Next, using a solvent-wetted brush, run it the full length of the bore as many times as is necessary to completely dislodge all foreign matter from the bore and chamber. Dry the bore with clean patches and examine it. If the bore remains fouled, repeat the brushing. Complete the cleaning by dry-patch wiping the bore and chamber.
steps.cite: MARLIN® MODEL 1895™ AND MODEL 336™ LEVER-ACTION RIFLES INSTRUCTION MANUAL — MCLA 1/2026 R8 (document PM733) — Care and Cleaning — p.34

steps.title: Bolt body and both firing pins, then prove the rear pin
steps.action: Spray and brush the bolt body, get cleaner around BOTH the front and rear firing pins, then dry it properly — compressed air if you have it. Oil lightly inside and out, then push the rear firing pin in and let it go. It must move freely and return fully downward on its own; if it does not, clean it again and re-test.
steps.prose: This rifle uses a two-piece firing pin with a rear pin that acts as the lever-position safety. A sticky rear pin is not a nuisance, it is a defect.
steps.quote:
5. Ensure the firing pin spring is present and the rear firing pin moves freely by
pushing on the rear firing pin. 6. If the rear firing pin does not move freely, repeat steps 1 through 5. See Figure 20.
steps.cite: MARLIN® MODEL 1895™ AND MODEL 336™ LEVER-ACTION RIFLES INSTRUCTION MANUAL — MCLA 1/2026 R8 (document PM733) — To Clean the Bolt Assembly — p.36
steps.warn: If the rear firing pin does not return fully downward after being depressed, then your firearm is NOT in a safe operating condition and it must NOT be used until you have it inspected and the problem corrected by the factory.

steps.title: Inside the receiver and the ejector
steps.action: Spray and brush everything you can reach inside the receiver, and do the ejector the same way. Dry both thoroughly, then put a light film of oil inside and outside the receiver and on the ejector. Wipe the excess off — oil left standing in a lever action collects grit and that is what causes the sluggish, gritty lever people blame on wear.
steps.quote: 3. Use a clean, solvent-wetted patch to remove firing residue and dirt from all “reachable” surfaces inside the receiver. Use the solvent-wetted toothbrush to dislodge residue from all parts of the bolt assembly and from surfaces inside the receiver that can’t be reached with a patch. Use cleaning patches or the cloth to remove the solvent.
steps.cite: MARLIN® MODEL 1895™ AND MODEL 336™ LEVER-ACTION RIFLES INSTRUCTION MANUAL — MCLA 1/2026 R8 (document PM733) — Care and Cleaning — p.34

steps.title: Light oil everywhere, and very little of it
steps.action: Wipe every surface, inside and out, with a very light coat of oil, then wipe the excess back off. A drop on the bolt components, on the trigger mechanism's pivot points and on the safety will work its way into everything that needs it. More oil is not more protection — it is a dirt magnet in an action that runs open to the weather.
steps.quote: 4. Wipe all surfaces – internal and external – with a very light coat of oil. Oil and similar preparations “collect” dirt particles that can interfere with reliable functioning of the rifle. Therefore, use these preparations very sparingly. A drop of oil applied to the bolt assembly components, the pivot points of the trigger mechanism, and the safety, will work into all the parts that need lubrication.
steps.cite: MARLIN® MODEL 1895™ AND MODEL 336™ LEVER-ACTION RIFLES INSTRUCTION MANUAL — MCLA 1/2026 R8 (document PM733) — Care and Cleaning — p.34
steps.warn: Firing a rifle with oil, grease, or any other material even partially obstructing the bore may result in damage to the rifle and serious injury to the shooter and those nearby.

deepSteps.title: Butt stock mounting screw out of the tang
deepSteps.action: The deep clean starts at the tang. Find the butt stock mounting screw on the tang behind the hammer — the tang screw — and turn it counterclockwise all the way out. It is a long screw running down through the wrist, so give it plenty of turns and do not stop when it feels free; it is still engaged.
deepSteps.quote:
10. Remove the butt stock mounting screw located on the tang behind the
hammer (sometimes called the tang screw) by turning it counterclockwise. See Figure 18.
deepSteps.cite: MARLIN® MODEL 1895™ AND MODEL 336™ LEVER-ACTION RIFLES INSTRUCTION MANUAL — MCLA 1/2026 R8 (document PM733) — To Remove the Butt Stock — p.33

deepSteps.title: Butt stock straight back off the receiver
deepSteps.action: Grip the receiver in one hand and the butt stock in the other and pull them apart along the axis of the rifle. It comes straight back — no twisting, no rocking. The wrist of a lever-gun stock is thin where it meets the tang and levering it sideways is how it cracks.
deepSteps.quote: 11. With a firm grip on the receiver and butt stock, pull the butt stock from the receiver. See Figure 19.
deepSteps.cite: MARLIN® MODEL 1895™ AND MODEL 336™ LEVER-ACTION RIFLES INSTRUCTION MANUAL — MCLA 1/2026 R8 (document PM733) — To Remove the Butt Stock — p.33

deepSteps.title: Trigger and hammer cleaned AS A UNIT — nothing comes out
deepSteps.action: With the stock off, the fire control is exposed but it stays in the rifle. Cock the hammer to its second, full-cock position, then flood inside the receiver with gun cleaner — a spray straw makes this controllable. Do NOT drive out the hammer or trigger pins; Marlin cleans this group in place and takes it no further.
deepSteps.prose: This is the boundary between deep clean and gunsmithing on this rifle, and it is stated on the page rather than implied.
deepSteps.quote: NOTE: Clean and lubricate the trigger and hammer assemblies as a unit. Do not remove the hammer or the trigger assembly from the receiver.
deepSteps.cite: MARLIN® MODEL 1895™ AND MODEL 336™ LEVER-ACTION RIFLES INSTRUCTION MANUAL — MCLA 1/2026 R8 (document PM733) — To Clean and Lubricate the Trigger & Hammer — p.37

deepSteps.title: Work the safety, then dry the receiver out
deepSteps.action: While the cleaner is in there, move the safety mechanism from SAFE to FIRE and back several times so the solvent gets carried through the crossbolt's bore and around the locking bolt. Then dry the receiver thoroughly — compressed air if you have it, otherwise let it air dry completely before any oil goes near it. Solvent trapped under oil in a blind hole is how a lever gun starts rusting from the inside.
deepSteps.quote:
2. Move the safety mechanism from the "SAFE" to "FIRE" position multiple times.
3. Air dry or use compressed air to thoroughly dry the receiver assembly.
deepSteps.cite: MARLIN® MODEL 1895™ AND MODEL 336™ LEVER-ACTION RIFLES INSTRUCTION MANUAL — MCLA 1/2026 R8 (document PM733) — To Clean and Lubricate the Trigger & Hammer — p.37

deepSteps.title: Prove the locking bolt moves freely
deepSteps.action: Push the locking bolt from the BOTTOM of the receiver and watch it move. It must travel freely; if it is sticky, go back and repeat the cleaning and drying until it is not. The locking bolt is what holds the breech shut behind a .30-30 or .45-70 case head, so free movement here is a safety check and not a smoothness preference.
deepSteps.quote: 4. Ensure the locking bolt moves freely by pushing the locking bolt from the bottom of the receiver. See Figure 22.
deepSteps.cite: MARLIN® MODEL 1895™ AND MODEL 336™ LEVER-ACTION RIFLES INSTRUCTION MANUAL — MCLA 1/2026 R8 (document PM733) — To Clean and Lubricate the Trigger & Hammer — p.37

deepSteps.title: Four lubrication points, lightly
deepSteps.action: Marlin identifies exactly four points to lubricate in this group, illustrated in Figures 23 and 24, and asks for a light application at each. Put oil on those points and nowhere else — the receiver interior does not want a bath, and surplus oil here runs down into the stock inletting and softens the wood over time.
deepSteps.quote: 6. Lightly lubricate each of the four (4) points as shown in Figures 23 and 24, below.
deepSteps.cite: MARLIN® MODEL 1895™ AND MODEL 336™ LEVER-ACTION RIFLES INSTRUCTION MANUAL — MCLA 1/2026 R8 (document PM733) — To Clean and Lubricate the Trigger & Hammer — p.37

cleaning.name: Bore and chamber
tasks: Rod in from the CHAMBER end only; solvent-wet patch through to the muzzle several times.
Correct-calibre brush, full length of the bore, as many passes as the fouling needs.
Never reverse the rod while a brush or patch is in the bore — it binds.
Dry patches until they come out clean, then a lightly oiled patch, then a dry one.
Clean the chamber and the extractor as often as needed — bullet lubricant building up in the chamber is Marlin's own named cause of failures to extract.

cleaning.name: Bolt assembly
tasks: Spray and brush the bolt body with gun cleaner.
Cleaner around BOTH the front and rear firing pins.
Dry thoroughly — compressed air if available.
Light oil inside and outside the bolt, on the firing pins and on the firing pin spring.
Confirm the firing pin spring is present and the rear firing pin returns fully downward on its own.

cleaning.name: Receiver and ejector
tasks: Spray and brush every component reachable inside the receiver.
Spray and, if needed, brush the ejector; do not bend it.
Dry the receiver and ejector thoroughly.
Light oil inside and outside the receiver and on the ejector.

cleaning.name: Exterior and stock
tasks: Test any cleaning agent in an inconspicuous area before using it on a finished surface.
No caustic or acetone-based cleaners; on wood or laminate stocks acetone will damage the finish.
Wipe external metal dry after use or exposure; a light film of oil or preservative for storage.

reassembly: If the butt stock came off: stock back onto the receiver first, then the tang screw down through the wrist and tightened.
Ejector back into its seat in the receiver, receiver still lying ejection-port-UP.
Bolt assembly in from the rear, straight along its rails until it is home.
Bolt pushed forward to roughly half closed so the lever can pick it up.
Lever up into the receiver and into the bolt assembly, then rotated to its half-stroke position.
Lever mounting screw in and tightened.
Wipe off all excess solvent, lubricant and preservative before the rifle goes away or gets loaded.
fncheck: With the rifle proven empty and the muzzle in a safe direction: cycle the lever through several full strokes and confirm it opens and closes with no binding and that the bolt locks up when the lever is fully closed. Push the safety button fully right and confirm the red band disappears, then fully left and confirm it reappears. Push the rear firing pin in and release it — it must return fully downward on its own, and if it does not, the rifle is not in safe operating condition and must go to the factory. Push the locking bolt from beneath the receiver and confirm it moves freely. Finally, check the bore is clear of patches, oil and obstructions before the rifle is loaded.
